title: Can a CPA Represent You Before the IRS? Rules and Form 2848
metaDescription: A CPA can represent a taxpayer before the IRS with unlimited rights under Circular 230, once authorized on Form 2848, covering audits, appeals, and collections.
h1: Can a CPA Represent a Taxpayer Before the IRS?
cardBlurb: A Certified Public Accountant holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS under Circular 230 once authorized on Form 2848, covering audits, collections, and appeals.
introText:
A Certified Public Accountant (CPA) can represent a taxpayer before the [Internal Revenue Service (IRS)](https://www.irs.gov) on any tax matter. The CPA must be in good standing and authorized on Form 2848. Along with attorneys and Enrolled Agents, CPAs hold unlimited practice rights under federal regulations.

That authority allows a CPA to communicate directly with IRS personnel, appear at examination meetings, negotiate payment arrangements, and take disputes before the [IRS Independent Office of Appeals](https://www.irs.gov/appeals). The taxpayer need not attend those meetings.

A CPA cannot simply call the IRS or attend an audit on a taxpayer's behalf without written authorization. That authorization is specific. The agency will not disclose confidential records or recognize the CPA's legal authority to act without it.

sections.heading: What Circular 230 Authorizes a CPA to Do
sections.body:
Under [Circular 230](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/circular-230-tax-professionals), a CPA who is duly qualified to practice in any U.S. state, territory, possession, commonwealth, or the District of Columbia holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS. The CPA must not be suspended or disbarred. Three credentials share this same authority: CPAs, attorneys, and Enrolled Agents. Each group completes different education, licensing exams, and jurisdictional requirements. Their scope of practice before the IRS does not differ. Any of the three can handle any taxpayer matter, regardless of who prepared the original return.

Unenrolled return preparers face tighter rules. The IRS outlines these distinctions in its guidance on [tax return preparer credentials and qualifications](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/understanding-tax-return-preparer-credentials-and-qualifications). An individual who participates in the IRS Annual Filing Season Program holds limited representation rights only. That preparer may represent only the taxpayers whose returns they personally prepared and signed. Their authority is further restricted to discussions before IRS customer service representatives, revenue agents, and similar frontline personnel. An Annual Filing Season Program participant cannot represent a taxpayer in an IRS appeals conference or handle collection matters.

Some preparers have no standing at all. A preparer holding only an active Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN), without completing the Annual Filing Season Program or holding a recognized credential, has had no IRS representation authority since January 1, 2016. That holds even if the preparer prepared the return in question. A taxpayer weighing these options can review the detailed [tax attorney vs CPA vs Enrolled Agent](/compare/tax-attorney-vs-cpa-vs-enrolled-agent/) comparison.

sections.heading: Form 2848 as the Official Authorization Mechanism
sections.body:
IRS [Form 2848](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-2848), titled Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, is the formal document that authorizes an eligible professional to represent a taxpayer before the IRS. It grants two distinct legal powers. The representative may inspect and receive the taxpayer's confidential tax return information, and may perform legal acts the taxpayer could perform, such as signing agreements, consents, or waivers on the specified matters. Form 2848 also covers Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) examinations, in addition to standard federal tax matters.

Form 2848 is not a blanket grant of authority. Part I of the form requires the taxpayer to identify the exact tax matters, the specific tax form numbers, and the precise years or accounting periods covered by the authorization. Because the authorization is strictly scoped to the listed matters and periods, a CPA authorized for an audit of one specific tax year has no standing to speak with the IRS regarding a different, unlisted year, even if the underlying accounting dispute is identical. When an examination expands to adjacent tax years, the taxpayer must submit a new or amended Form 2848 naming those additional periods before the CPA can take action on them.

Eligibility extends beyond CPAs and attorneys. The [Instructions for Form 2848](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i2848) list several categories of eligible representatives: CPAs, attorneys, Enrolled Agents, Enrolled Actuaries, Enrolled Retirement Plan Agents, corporate officers representing an organization, full-time employees, certain family members (spouse, parent, child, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, and corresponding step-relations), unenrolled return preparers for returns they prepared, and qualifying students or law graduates working in a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic (LITC) or Student Tax Clinic Program (STCP).

Completing Form 2848 also requires Part II, the Declaration of Representative. There, the CPA states their designation as a CPA and attests to three things: current authorization to practice, awareness of the applicable Circular 230 responsibilities, and authorization to represent the taxpayer for the matters listed on the form. A separate identifier, the Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number, tracks the representative in IRS records. The CAF number is a unique nine-digit number the IRS assigns to authorized representatives, distinct from a Social Security number, an Employer Identification Number, a Preparer Tax Identification Number, or an enrollment card number.

sections.heading: Form 2848 vs Form 8821: Representation vs Information Authorization
sections.body:
Form 2848 differs sharply from IRS [Form 8821](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8821), titled Tax Information Authorization. Both forms grant access to confidential tax data. Their legal scope is not the same. Form 8821 authorizes a designated appointee solely to inspect or receive confidential tax return information from the IRS. It does not grant any power of attorney. The recipient cannot speak on the taxpayer's behalf, advocate positions, answer examination questions, or negotiate settlements with the IRS.

Form 2848 includes all the disclosure access of Form 8821, and adds full representation rights on top of it. A representative named on Form 2848 can negotiate directly with the IRS and can also sign agreements, consents, or waivers on the specified tax matters. If a taxpayer only needs a third party to inspect tax information, Form 8821 serves that purpose without conferring legal agency. Whenever a professional must respond to an IRS examiner, handle a collection matter, or argue a disputed issue before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, Form 2848 is required.

sections.heading: How to File Form 2848
sections.body:
The IRS accepts Form 2848 three ways. Taxpayers can file it online, by fax, or by mail. The online option is the official portal at [IRS.gov/Submit2848](https://www.irs.gov/submit2848), which allows taxpayers and representatives to upload completed forms and supports electronic signatures.

Taxpayers and practitioners who do not use the online tool must submit the completed form by fax or postal mail. The correct fax number and mailing address depend directly on the taxpayer's geographic location, as detailed in the Instructions for Form 2848. The IRS instructions do not state a filing fee for processing Form 2848. There is no indicated agency fee to record or maintain the power of attorney on the IRS Centralized Authorization File system. A taxpayer evaluating resolution strategies while submitting authorization documents can review estimated procedural costs with a [tax resolution calculator](/tax-resolution/).

sections.heading: Scope and Boundaries of CPA IRS Representation
sections.body:
Once the IRS processes a valid Form 2848 and records it on the CAF system, the CPA can manage the designated matter directly with the IRS. The CPA can attend audit meetings, respond to IRS correspondence, and challenge proposed adjustments. The CPA can also pursue the matter through IRS collection channels or through an administrative appeal before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals.

That representation authority stops at the IRS itself. A CPA's unlimited rights are confined to the executive branch and do not extend to federal courts. Representation in the United States Tax Court requires separate admission under the court's own rules, a point explored in the guide on [whether an Enrolled Agent can represent a taxpayer in Tax Court](/guides/can-an-enrolled-agent-represent-you-in-tax-court/). Representation rules also vary among the other categories eligible on Form 2848. A qualifying student or law graduate working in a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic (LITC) or Student Tax Clinic Program (STCP) is a narrower case. That representative's authorization automatically expires 130 days after the taxpayer signs the form, and the IRS then purges that student representative from the system. That 130-day auto-expiration rule applies only to the student clinic category.

This is general information about IRS practice standards, not legal or tax advice. A taxpayer facing an audit, collection notice, or proposed adjustment should evaluate the specific case with a licensed CPA, tax attorney, or Enrolled Agent.

faqs.question: Can a CPA represent a client before the IRS?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Treasury Circular 230, a Certified Public Accountant in good standing holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS. A CPA can represent a client on any tax matter, including audits, collection actions, and administrative appeals, regardless of who originally prepared the tax return.

faqs.question: Does a taxpayer need to file Form 2848 for a CPA to speak with the IRS on their behalf?
faqs.answer: Yes. The IRS requires a processed Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative, before agency personnel can disclose confidential tax information to a CPA or recognize the CPA's legal authority to advocate, negotiate, or execute agreements on the taxpayer's behalf.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Form 2848 and Form 8821?
faqs.answer: Form 2848 authorizes a representative to both inspect confidential tax records and legally act or speak on the taxpayer's behalf before the IRS. Form 8821 only authorizes a designated party to inspect or receive confidential tax records, granting no power to represent, negotiate, or advocate.

faqs.question: What is a CAF number?
faqs.answer: A Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number is a unique nine-digit identification number assigned by the IRS to an authorized representative. It is used by the IRS to track third-party authorizations and is separate from a Social Security number, Employer Identification Number, or PTIN.

faqs.question: Can Form 2848 be filed online?
faqs.answer: Yes. Form 2848 can be submitted online through the IRS submission tool at IRS.gov/Submit2848, which supports electronic signatures. Filers can also transmit the form via fax or postal mail to specific IRS locations based on the taxpayer's state of residence.

faqs.question: Is there a fee to file Form 2848?
faqs.answer: The IRS instructions for Form 2848 do not state a filing fee. There is no indicated agency fee charged by the IRS to submit, process, or record the power of attorney authorization on the Centralized Authorization File system.
